document_title: CBD COP 9 Decision IX/16 C — Ocean Fertilization
notes: CBD COP 9 Decision IX/16 C is the Convention on Biological Diversity's first explicit international policy response to ocean fertilization as a climate-related intervention. It urges Parties and other governments, consistent with the precautionary approach, to ensure that ocean-fertilization activities do not take place until there is an adequate scientific basis for judging the risks and an effective global, transparent and science-based control and regulatory mechanism is in place. The decision allows only small-scale scientific research studies within coastal waters, subject to rigorous prior assessment and only where justified by the need to gather specific scientific data. It also states that such research should not be used for generating or selling carbon offsets or for any other commercial purpose. In the Röschel and Neumann governance review, this decision is part of the direct policy response that complements the London Convention/London Protocol regime. It is a non-binding COP decision: it does not itself issue a project permit, establish a carbon-credit methodology, quantify net CO2 removal, or authorize commercial ocean-fertilization deployment.
source: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
status_note: Adopted by CBD COP 9 in 2008; non-binding international COP decision that remains an important precautionary governance reference for ocean fertilization.

document_title: Resolution LC-LP.1(2008) on the Regulation of Ocean Fertilization
notes: Resolution LC-LP.1(2008) is the first joint London Convention/London Protocol resolution specifically addressing ocean fertilization. The Parties agreed that the scope of the two dumping instruments includes ocean-fertilization activities and concluded that ocean fertilization other than legitimate scientific research should be considered contrary to the aims of the Convention and Protocol and should not currently qualify for an exemption from the definition of dumping. The resolution therefore established a strong precautionary presumption against non-research ocean fertilization while leaving a narrowly framed research pathway to be developed through further assessment rules. Röschel and Neumann identify this resolution as a central component of the direct and explicit international governance of ocean-based negative-emissions technologies. The resolution is policy guidance adopted by Parties rather than a self-executing global project permit. It does not authorize commercial deployment, does not establish removal accounting or carbon-credit issuance, and does not by itself prove the climatic effectiveness or permanence of ocean fertilization.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Convention/Protocol
status_note: Adopted jointly by London Convention and London Protocol Parties in 2008; non-binding resolution that remains a core precautionary policy reference for ocean fertilization.

document_title: Resolution LC-LP.2(2010) — Assessment Framework for Scientific Research Involving Ocean Fertilization
notes: Resolution LC-LP.2(2010) adopted the Assessment Framework for Scientific Research Involving Ocean Fertilization. The framework operationalizes the research exception recognized in the 2008 resolution by providing a structured, case-by-case process for deciding whether a proposal qualifies as legitimate scientific research. It requires a scientific rationale, characterization of the proposed activity, environmental assessment, risk management, monitoring, consideration of potential impacts and uncertainties, and follow-up before an activity should proceed. The framework is designed to distinguish genuine scientific research from activities that are effectively commercial or insufficiently justified and to reduce environmental harm while knowledge remains incomplete. Röschel and Neumann highlight this assessment framework as the most developed procedural instrument in the direct governance of ocean-based negative-emissions research. It is an assessment and safeguard framework, not evidence that ocean fertilization is effective at durable net CO2 removal, not a carbon-credit methodology, and not a blanket authorization for field deployment.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Convention/Protocol
status_note: Adopted by London Convention/London Protocol Parties in 2010 as the assessment framework for legitimate scientific ocean-fertilization research.

document_title: Resolution LP.4(8) — Amendment to Regulate Ocean Fertilization and Other Marine Geoengineering
notes: Resolution LP.4(8), adopted in 2013, amends the London Protocol to create a treaty-based control system for marine geoengineering. It adds Article 6bis, establishes a positive-list approach under which marine-geoengineering activities covered by a new annex may not be permitted unless they are listed, and provides an environmental assessment and permitting framework in Annex 5. Ocean fertilization is the first activity listed for regulation, with legitimate scientific research capable of being considered under the assessment framework while other listed activities would require future amendment decisions. The architecture is designed to be expandable to additional marine-geoengineering techniques. Röschel and Neumann treat the amendment as the key prospective international legal structure for governing marine CDR that involves placement of matter in the ocean. The amendment has been adopted but has not entered into force, so its treaty amendments are not yet operative internationally. It does not authorize commercial ocean fertilization, establish carbon-crediting rules, or validate the effectiveness, permanence or net climate benefit of any marine CDR pathway.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Protocol
status_note: Adopted in 2013; the marine-geoengineering amendment has not entered into force internationally.

document_title: Global Ocean Negative Carbon Emission (Global ONCE) — UN Ocean Decade Programme
notes: Global Ocean Negative Carbon Emission (Global-ONCE) is an endorsed UN Decade of Ocean Science programme led by Xiamen University, with an official programme period from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2030. The Ocean Decade description states that the programme will undertake and facilitate the science needed to evaluate and implement eco-technological interventions that could enhance ocean carbon sequestration, including restoration of impacted marine ecosystems, land-sea integrated management, manipulation of upwelling, microbial-driven carbon sequestration, and adjustment of nutrients, dissolved oxygen and pH. Its institutional functions are broader than a single technology project: it is intended to build an international network of field stations and research facilities, co-design interdisciplinary research, develop an evaluation framework for mitigation and adaptation approaches, coordinate capacity building, and improve equitable policy, governance and societal understanding. A 2025 peer-reviewed declaration by early-career ocean professionals describes Global-ONCE as a platform spanning 79 research groups in 33 countries and more than 1,500 participants and calls for stronger basic and applied mCDR research, blue-carbon protection and restoration, international cooperation, monitoring, capacity building and attention to precaution and equity. These descriptions support classification as a research, coordination and evidence-building programme. They do not constitute blanket legal authorization for ocean CDR deployment, do not certify a carbon-credit methodology, and do not establish a quantified programme-wide carbon-removal obligation or guarantee that any intervention will be environmentally acceptable or commercially deployable.
source: UNESCO-IOC Ocean Decade

This framework is therefore regulatory and precautionary rather than a blanket authorization for ocean alkalinity enhancement, ocean fertilization, biomass sinking or other interventions. Any individual project remains subject to the applicable statutory pathway, site-specific review, environmental safeguards, public-process requirements and other federal or state approvals. The guidance does not create a carbon-crediting methodology, establish removal factors, certify permanence, or determine whether any specific marine CDR approach is environmentally acceptable.

document_title: CREW Carbon–Microsoft Wastewater Alkalinity Enhancement Carbon Removal Offtake Agreement
notes: CREW Carbon announced on 4 August 2026 an offtake agreement with Microsoft for delivery of up to 23,602 durable verified carbon-removal units from CREW's wastewater alkalinity enhancement technology. document_title: Kvina River CDR Project — Isometric-Validated River Alkalinity Enhancement with Ocean DIC Storage
notes: CarbonRun’s Kvina River CDR Project adds finely crushed natural alkaline rock to the Kvina River, increasing alkalinity and converting dissolved CO2 to bicarbonate; the bicarbonate is transported to the ocean for millennial-scale marine storage. Isometric lists the project as validated, with approval on 20 January 2026. At the 16 August 2026 audit point, the registry displayed 76.69 issued certificates, 22.002 retired certificates and 1.534 certificates in the buffer pool, with a crediting period from 15 May 2025 to 15 May 2030. The project is included because the accounting pathway explicitly terminates in ocean DIC storage; it should not be generalized to conventional river liming or acidification mitigation. The certificates are voluntary-registry units, not a Norwegian compliance-market offset or blanket authorization for river dosing elsewhere.
source: Isometric / CarbonRun
status_note: Validated by Isometric; approval date 20 January 2026; active crediting period through 15 May 2030. Registry quantities are point-in-time values checked 16 August 2026.

document_title: Carbon to Sea USD 225,000 Award — Integrating Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement with Municipal Wastewater Treatment
notes: On 23 July 2026, Carbon to Sea awarded USD 225,000 to a cross-sector team led by the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science to evaluate integration of Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement (OAE) with municipal wastewater-treatment technologies, explicitly including Wastewater Alkalinity Enhancement (WAE). This is a funded research-and-policy implementation practice, not authorization for a specific discharge and not evidence that all wastewater alkalinity management produces durable CDR.
